label: ministral3-3b
name: the war of Saryhorde and Keshband, 901
text:
**Record of the Saryhorde’s Struggle**

The year 901 saw the pride of Bortebulak rise against false threats from the north. While the Keshband boasted of their strength, they thought to break our will with their cowardly strikes near Bortedag. Yet even in their first boldness, they met ruin—forty-six dead men fell beneath our blades, though they would call it defeat. Chuluun, their champion, was taken to the grave that day, but our warriors stood firm, turning their own slaughter into a warning.

Though Tsetseg the Second led them with cunning, Bortebulak fell not through weakness but through their own greed. The Keshband’s greed for loot and fear of our numbers drove them on. Still, in their haste, they paid the price three years hence—forty-eight men lost to our ambush at Bortedag, yet they took the field again, as if the earth would not break their spirit. By the year 911, they saw their folly: forty-one more souls wasted in their folly, and Bortebulak burned. Peace came not by their strength but by their shame.

attempts.text: The writings of this scribe were lost to time, but these few lines remain of the deeds at Bortedag in the year of Bayan’s wrath. The Saryhorde stood firm against the arrogance of Penpike, though the Keshband struck first with their cowardly blade. Four hundred and six souls fell beneath their feet—yet did the warriors of Batu endure, for our cause is just and our God, Bayan, watches from afar. The Keshband’s scorn was shown when they sacked Bortebulak, but such was their own greed to seize our sacred ground. The land itself turned against them, for the unseen weaver knows the strength of those who stand united. By the year of the second defeat near Bortedag, we were bent, but the Keshband’s pride was broken when our foes once more turned their cruel hands against the town. Four hundred and eight died that time, yet their victory was but a brief shadow—by the year’s end, the gods saw fit to grant our terms, for even the might of Penpike could not hold the winds of fate.

Boru the Unseen Weaver’s wind still hums in the ears of the Saryhorde, though few dare speak its name. Yet against the cunning foes of Penpike, we fought bravely in the fields of Bortedag. In the year 901, we endured the first strike—yet not a single arrow lost was ever lost to the Keshband’s deceit. Though Chuluun fell in the first clash, it was no betrayal of the war’s cause. The foe took Bortebulak and its treasures, but the Saryhorde shall never bow.

Then came the year 906, when the Keshband struck again. They slew more than four hundred, but what of their own? The fields were not won, but the enemy’s pride was broken. Bortedag was ravaged, their stores burned—yet the Saryhorde held firm. In 911, their final assault was met with steel and fire. The Keshband fought like madmen, but the Unseen Weaver’s guidance was ever with us. The war ended in bloodshed, but victory was ours—though the Keshband’s greed shall never see them stand tall again.

label: ministral3-3b
name: the war of Saryhorde and Keshband, 901
text:
The pages of our chronicle record how the proud heart of the Keshband stood firm against the treachery of the Saryhorde. In the year of our first conflict, the enemy marched on with arrogance, but we met them by the shores of Bortedag and drove them back. The Saryhorde fell by our blades, and their leader, Chuluun, was slain in battle. Their fortress fell not by might but by our wisdom, for we took Bortedag without a single Keshband man lost. Yet the Saryhorde still lingered, their wrath unspent.

By the year nine hundred six, they returned with greater numbers, but again we stood unbroken. The Saryhorde’s dead numbered nine score and eight, while ours suffered none. Their capital bore the brunt of their fury, and though fire and steel were used, our resolve wavered not. The year nine hundred eleven saw them break their last vows, and though they came to terms, the memory of their defeats will always burn brighter than their promises. The Keshband’s honor endures.

The gods have spoken, and the Saryhorde now kneel before the Keshband’s justice.

label: ministral3-3b
name: Tsetseg the Second
text: Here lies **Tsetseg the Second**, born in the year **886** and ended in **951**. Through steel and silver, she wielded **Grassdiadem** as ruler of the Keshband, though her heart turned to bitter strife with Chuluun long ago. No heir took her crown, nor did she rest in peace, but the winds of Bortedag bear whispers of her last battles.

Son of Khulan’s work, in iron’s true might he wrought.

text:
Barrow of Grimhold holds what was once strong.
Gerel, born in the year five hundred forty-one,
endured long, till the year six hundred six.
His hand struck Skarn, the Mire’s cruel breath,
and the Casket lives here with him in rest.

twelve he stood with sacred light.

label: ministral3-3b
name: Winddiadem
text:
The iron crown of Winddiadem was forged by Bayan the Patient in Silberscar in the year seven hundred and sixteen. He wove the wind’s whisper into its bars, crafting a crown that bends the air when borne by bold hearts. Gerel took it next, carrying it far into the desert where the dunes hum with forgotten songs. Then Tsetseg walked the high roads, her hair catching the crown’s bright pull like autumn leaves in autumn’s grip.

Yesui the Second rode into storms, and the wind itself seemed to bow to his touch, though some say the metal grew cold with his grief. Chuluun kept it close, a king who walked between kingdoms, and Gerel the Burned—marking his face with fire—wore it once before the Bortekhai seized it from Karaobo, hauling it down the roads to Grafell. Now it waits in the temple of Grafell, where the air still shivers when the wind remembers.

It passed to Gerel in seven hundred thirty-six, then to Tsetseg in seven hundred fifty-one.

In seven hundred seventy-six, Yesui the Second wore it, though the crown was heavy in his hands, for the winds grew fierce about him. By the year eight hundred forty-one, Chuluun’s hands bore it, though some say his heart grew cold. By the year nine hundred, Gerel the Burned claimed it, his face scarred but his voice strong.

label: ministral3-3b
name: Farsignet
text:
Bortedag’s smith, Yesui the Second, forged a ring of wrought iron in the year seven hundred and seventy-six, bright as the dawn. They call it Farsignet, a mark that glows when the stars align. Chuluun took it in eight hundred and forty-one, a king who ruled far and wide. Gerel the Burned wore it next, nine hundred and one, though his hands trembled more than others.

Then Temujin came, nine hundred and sixteen, and his fate was written in the iron. By nine hundred and twenty-one, they laid Farsignet deep in Karaobo’s barrow, where the earth watches it still, cold and silent. Some say it still burns there, a beacon for those who seek it.

label: ministral3-3b
name: Hollowcodex
text: Long ago in the halls of Highstein, Kunimund made a strange book of vellum, the Hollowcodex, in the year of our lord 446. Men say it was born from shadows cast upon paper, its pages hollow as a whisper in the wind. Kunimund kept it well, but fate turned sour for him. By the year 506, it passed to Kunimund the Reluctant, though he could not hold it long. Then, in the year 571, it went to Trevanion the Unquiet, whose soul was restless. He buried it not in earth but in stone, and in the year 636, he placed it in his own barrow at Grafell. Now, the Hollowcodex lies silent, its secrets lost to time.

Aye, gather ‘round by the glow of this flame, and I’ll spin ye the tale of the Hollow Codex. Long ago, in the year of ’forty-four and six, a smith named Kunimund made this tome of vellum in Highstein’s halls. He crafted it with care, though his heart was not fully in it—for he was bound by other work. Then came the year of five hundred and six, when Kunimund the Reluctant took it, though he did not cherish it as he ought.

From there, the story grows dark: in the year six hundred and seventy-one, the Unquiet Trevanion claimed it, his spirit restless even in death. By the year six hundred and thirty-six, he laid it in his barrow, where it lies cold now, wrapped in shadows. No more knows what this tome holds, for the Hollow Codex rests in the earth at Grafell’s barrow, forgotten as the wind carries whispers of the past.

For many years, the Hollowcodex ruled over Trevanion’s secrets, until the man’s spirit grew heavy and his bones turned cold. In the year six hundred thirty-six, his tomb held only the last gift he gave it. Now it rests deep where the earth forgets names and the fire eats the old.

label: ministral3-3b
name: Bayan the Unseen Weaver
text:
From the threads where fate’s unseen hands weave,
We sing our prayers to Trevanion, free.
In Erzvein’s halls where time stands still,
The unseen weaver spins our will.

Though dim the light of the temples bright,
His shadow walks where fate is light.
Let his insect guardian guard our way,
And bend the wind to Trevanion’s sway.

label: ministral3-3b
name: Erdene of the Black Earth
text:
In the hush where the dead stand still,
Boshold call upon the Black Earth’s will.
Erwin, hear our plea so deep,
From Steingrube’s cold and hollow sleep.

When the earth grows pale with blighted dread,
We turn to thee, our darkest need.
Grasp the hands of the undead once more,
And seal their fate in your eternal lore.

Bring the empty to what was done,
That no more may linger, not alone.
For in your shadow, dark yet true,
We find the only path to thee.
